# Intrinsic reflection correlation: exact parity and moment identities

Let C be a compact convex subset of R^n x R^d, let

    S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) != empty,
    q=dim_H(S),  mu=H_q restricted to S,  M=mu(S).

The body may have lower-dimensional integer fibers with different affine
direction spaces. Put K_z={x:(z,x) in C}, and let

    P={z in Z^n: dim aff(K_z)=q},
    w_z=H_q(K_z)>0 for z in P.

There are finitely many nonempty integer fibers, q is the largest of their
affine dimensions, and `0<M=sum_(z in P)w_z<infinity`. For q=0, H_0 is
counting measure, every nonempty fiber is one point, and P contains all
nonempty integer fibers. For q>0, smaller-dimensional fibers have zero
mu mass but remain in S when centers are considered.

For y=(j,x) in S, define its central-reflection retention by

    R(y)=H_q(S intersect (2y-S)).                      (1)

For each represented parity class r, put

    P_r={z in P:z mod 2=r},
    mu_r=mu restricted to the fibers P_r,
    M_r=mu_r(S),   m_r=integral y dmu_r(y).

All vector moments below use the full ambient coordinate y=(z,x).

## 1. Affine alignment at every contributing midpoint

Take z,w in P with the same parity and put j=(z+w)/2. Convexity gives

    (K_z+K_w)/2 subset K_j.                            (2)

Write L_z=lin(K_z-K_z), and similarly for w. The affine direction space
of K_z+K_w is L_z+L_w. Since both summands have dimension q and every
integer fiber has dimension at most q, (2) implies

    L_z=L_w=L_j=:L,    dim L=q,
    aff(K_j)=(aff(K_z)+aff(K_w))/2.                   (3)

Moreover `(K_z+K_w)/2` has positive H_q measure in that affine space:
each summand contains a relative ball, so their sum does as well.
Therefore j belongs to P. This proves the required direction alignment
without assuming a common direction space for all fibers. Distinct
parity classes can have different directions.

The statement includes q=0: the three fibers in (2) are singletons, and
the midpoint singleton is exactly their affine midpoint.

For a center y=(j,x), any term of positive H_q measure in (1) must pair
two fibers indexed by z,w=2j-z in P. A smaller-dimensional member makes
the intersection H_q-null. Consequently

    R(j,x)=sum_(z,w in P:z+w=2j)
                 H_q(K_z intersect (2x-K_w)).         (4)

This is an ORDERED-pair sum: each possible source fiber z contributes
once. In particular R=0 at every center in a fiber outside P.

## 2. Master identity for arbitrary test functions

For every nonnegative Borel function Phi on S, or every bounded Borel
function, one has

  integral_S Phi(y)R(y)dmu(y)
    =2^(-q) sum_r integral integral
                Phi((a+b)/2) dmu_r(a)dmu_r(b).         (5)

The right side uses independent, ordered endpoint pairs in the same
parity class. Their midpoints belong to S by convexity and parity.

To prove (5), fix z,w in P with the same parity and choose translations
so that `K_z=a+A`, `K_w=b+B`, with A,B in their common q-dimensional
Euclidean direction space L from (3). Parameterize the midpoint fiber
by `x=(a+b)/2+xi`, xi in L. Its contribution to (4) is

    integral_A 1_B(2xi-eta) dH_q(eta).

It is zero outside `(A+B)/2`, which lies in the midpoint fiber by (2).
Thus the xi integral over K_j can be extended to all of L. Tonelli and
the substitution `zeta=2xi-eta` give the Jacobian `d xi=2^(-q)d zeta`
and exactly the corresponding ordered-pair term of (5). Orthonormal
coordinates on L make this the usual q-dimensional change of variables;
there is no ambient-dimension Jacobian and no mismatch between affine
Hausdorff measures. Sum the finitely many terms. Bounded signed functions
follow by positive and negative parts.

For q=0, the same calculation is simply a finite sum with Jacobian one.
Each ordered pair contributes one unit at its actual integer midpoint.
No fractional-atom purification or continuous change of variables is
being used in that case.

## 3. Exact total correlation and first moments

Taking Phi=1 and then the ambient coordinate functions in (5) yields

    integral_S R dmu = 2^(-q) sum_r M_r^2,             (6)

    integral_S y R(y)dmu(y) = 2^(-q) sum_r M_r m_r.    (7)

Equation (6) is equivalently

    sum_(j in P) integral_(K_j) R(j,x)dH_q(x)
       =2^(-q) sum_r M_r^2.

For (7), the two terms a/2 and b/2 in each ordered-pair midpoint give
equal first moments. Boundary points are included everywhere. The
derivation does not discard lower-dimensional boundaries in the q=0
case or place positive q-volume on lower-dimensional integer fibers.

Put A=sum_r M_r^2 and g_r=m_r/M_r. The probability law

    d eta(y) = (2^q/A)R(y)dmu(y)                      (8)

is exactly obtained by choosing class r with probability `M_r^2/A`, then
choosing two independent points from `mu_r/M_r` and taking their midpoint.
Its centroid is

    g_eta = (sum_r M_r^2 g_r)/(sum_r M_r^2).           (9)

This is generally different from the original centroid
`sum_r M_r g_r/M`. In particular the identity does not assert a
centroid-preserving operation on the original mixed measure.

## 4. Attainment and the universal weak retention bound

The function R is upper semicontinuous on compact S. Indeed, for y in S,
reflection about y preserves Z^n x R^d, so (1) can also be written

    R(y)=integral_S 1_C(2y-a)dmu(a).                  (10)

If y_k tends to y in S, closedness of C gives pointwise
`limsup 1_C(2y_k-a)<=1_C(2y-a)`. Since the integrands are bounded by one
and mu is finite, the reversed Fatou inequality proves
`limsup R(y_k)<=R(y)`. This proof remains valid with positive boundary
mass and for q=0.

Consequently R attains its maximum on S. If p is the number of represented
parity classes, (6) and Cauchy--Schwarz imply

    R_max >= (sum_r M_r^2)/(2^q M)
          >= M/(2^q p)
          >= M/2^(n+q).                              (11)

Since the right side is positive, a maximizing center lies on a positive
q-dimensional fiber. The retained source in (1) is centrally symmetric
about its actual mixed center. Every closed halfspace containing that
center contains at least half of its retained H_q mass, including when
some of that mass lies on the cutting boundary. Thus (11) also supplies
the weaker depth certificate `2^(-(n+q+1))`. This is not the OC constant,
and no stronger mixed retention statement is inferred from convolution.

For q=0, (6) reduces exactly to the ordered-pair counting identity

    sum_(y in S) #(S intersect (2y-S))=sum_r #(S_r)^2.

## 5. An exact quadratic and convex-order consequence

For completeness, let `Q_r=integral yy^T dmu_r(y)`. The same master
identity gives

    integral yy^T R(y)dmu(y)
      =2^(-(q+1)) sum_r (M_r Q_r+m_r m_r^T).          (12)

Let `nu=A^(-1) sum_r M_r mu_r`. This probability measure and eta from
(8) have the same centroid. For every convex Borel function phi on conv(S)
whose integrals exist (in particular every continuous convex ambient test),
Jensen at each endpoint pair in (5) gives

    integral phi d eta <= integral phi d nu.          (13)

Writing `V_r=integral (y-g_r)(y-g_r)^T dmu_r(y)`, their covariance
matrices satisfy the exact relation

    Cov(nu)-Cov(eta)=(1/(2A)) sum_r M_r V_r >=0.       (14)

The source on the right of (13) is the explicitly parity-reweighted law
nu, not mu/M. Equations (12)--(14) give a precise one-step invariant;
they do not justify density-preserving iteration or any depth transfer
not separately proved.

## 6. Checks and relation to earlier notes

For the actual interval example with lengths `(2,6,10,3)` at bases
`0,1,2,3`, parity masses are 12 and 9. Direct integration of the complete
piecewise reflection formulas gives

    integral R dmu=225/2,
    integral zR dmu=375/2,
    integral xR dmu=1653/4,

in agreement with (6)--(7). The exact verifier is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_intrinsic_reflection_parity_correlation.py`.

Different fiber orientations are genuinely permitted. For example in
R x R^2, take C to be the convex hull of the segment
`{0} x ([0,2] x {0})` and the segment
`{1} x ({0} x [1,5])`. C is a full three-dimensional tetrahedron, and its
only integer fibers have q=1 with perpendicular directions. Their parity
classes differ, so each contributes its own ordinary one-dimensional
self-correlation; (6) gives `(2^2+4^2)/2=10`. Their full first moment in
(7) is `(8,2,24)`. This checks the necessity of pairwise affine alignment
rather than a falsely assumed global fiber direction.

An archive check found the related bounded-density construction in
`candidate 9af97e78b545b0b8`, but its endpoint
couplings are not the independent product laws here. The present exact
intrinsic reflection density and its mass/first-moment identities were
not stated there. The ordinary continuous covariogram identity is the
n=0 special case of (5); the proof above supplies the finite lattice and
varying-orientation bookkeeping explicitly.
